---
title: "Colors"
subtitle: "5-, 10-, and 20-color sequences, native cycling, and backgrounds"
jupyter: python3
---

Three sequences follow the same indigo, cyan, green, yellow, orange, and red
family in light and dark appearances. Light mode keeps bright greens and yellows
and warm orange-reds. The recipe samples linear RGB interpolation between six
reference colors at equal intervals. The five-color midpoint falls between green
and yellow; the longer sequences include more neighboring transitions.

Switch the page appearance to compare treatments. Choose the sequence with
`apply_layout(fig, appearance, colors=5)`. Plotly cycles from the first color
when there are more series than colors. These remain **CONVERGING** appearance
candidates. All analytical curves are illustrative, not measurements.

```{python}
#| include: false
import math
from IPython.display import HTML, display
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from design import CONFIG, SEQUENCES, apply_layout
from review import anchors, display_figure

def swatches(appearance, size):
    colors = SEQUENCES[appearance][size]
    items = "".join(
        f'<div style="flex:1 1 5rem;min-width:5rem">'
        f'<div style="height:2.5rem;background:{color};border-radius:.3rem"></div>'
        f'<div style="font-size:.8rem;padding:.3rem 0">{index + 1} · {color}</div>'
        '</div>'
        for index, color in enumerate(colors)
    )
    return HTML(f'<div role="group" aria-label="{appearance} {size} colors" '
                f'style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:.7rem">{items}</div>')

def cycling(appearance, size, count):
    x = [index / 80 for index in range(161)]
    fig = go.Figure()
    for index in range(count):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=x,
            y=[index + 0.3 * math.cos(2 * math.pi * value + index / 3)
               for value in x],
            mode="lines", name=f"Series {index + 1}",
        ))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{size} colors · {count} analytical series",
                      xaxis_title="Illustrative parameter",
                      yaxis_title="Illustrative offset + cosine")
    return apply_layout(fig, appearance, colors=size, kind="cartesian")
```

## 5 colors

Seven curves: series 6 and 7 reuse colors 1 and 2. The swatches list the current
hexadecimal values.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
for appearance in ("light", "dark"):
    display(swatches(appearance, 5))
```

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
for appearance in ("light", "dark"):
    display_figure(cycling(appearance, size=5, count=7), config=CONFIG)
```

## 20 colors

Twenty-two curves: series 21 and 22 reuse colors 1 and 2. Neighboring colors
are closer in dense figures; use native hover and legend toggles to identify
series. The figure author should explicitly define any semantic line styles.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
for appearance in ("light", "dark"):
    display(swatches(appearance, 20))
```

```{python}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
for appearance in ("light", "dark"):
    display_figure(cycling(appearance, size=20, count=22), config=CONFIG)
```

## Paper and plot backgrounds

Four presentation backgrounds remain as pairing references: `paper_bgcolor`
is the outer figure background and `plot_bgcolor` is the plotting surface.
Each sample uses one accent color; the sequence order above is unchanged.
The curves are analytical Rabi oscillation examples, not device measurements.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Tech Slate

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
for appearance in ("light", "dark"):
    display_figure(next(fig for fig in anchors(appearance) if fig.layout.title.text == "Tech Slate"), config=CONFIG)
```
